title: Katie Zacharia quits as White House press secretary five days into job
description: Katie Zacharia will be leaving her post as White House press secretary, just five days after her shaky public debut.US President Donald Trump told rep
body: Katie Zacharia will be leaving her post as White House press secretary, just five days after her shaky public debut.US President Donald Trump told reporters moments before news of her exit was announced that he had told her "you don't have to do this if you don't want to" and "honestly, if I were you, I'd reconsider".Zacharia faced heavy criticism for her first press briefing on Tuesday, which lasted less than 15 minutes and included only three questions from reporters.The 42-year-old spent the days following playing defence, fielding tough questions from news outlets about her credentials and preparedness for the job.Trump hinted at her impending exit early on Friday afternoon, during an impromptu news conference in front of the Marine One helicopter."I said, 'Is this for you, Katie? Because honestly, you don't need this'," Trump said."You don't have to be treated this badly," he continued, adding that he believed she had been treated "pretty nastily" by the media. Hours later, she praised Trump as "kind, wonderful, gracious, thoughtful, enthusiastic, and the most hardworking man" on X, writing that it had been an honour to work for him.As the November midterm elections, which will decide who controls the US Congress, draw closer, Democrats are seizing on Zacharia's abrupt departure as a sign of failure in the Republican White House."The White House Press Secretary is gone. Maga extremists continue to fall apart," the top Democrat in the House of Representatives, Hakeem Jeffries, posted on X.Zacharia appeared visibly nervous during her inaugural White House press briefing, in which she read talking points from a notebook, answered only a few questions and referred to her husband as the president.During the briefing, a reporter asked Zacharia - who had been called an attorney by Trump and others and who graduated from Pepperdine University's law school - about where she passed the bar exam. To practise law in the US, an attorney must be admitted to a state's bar association by passing a rigorous exam."When I was in China," she replied.After intense scrutiny and digging by the media, Zacharia admitted on Thursday that she did not pass the bar exam.She did say in a statement that she had practised international transaction law in China with the "appropriate credentials".  Questions about her legal credentials became a major talking point throughout the week, with Sean Hannity, from conservative-leaning Fox News, lobbing particularly pointed questions at her during an interview on Thursday.When she said she had not passed the bar, he replied: "Why didn't you just say, 'I never practiced law?'"Zacharia also described how quickly she had taken on the press secretary role - having been hired less than a week before her debut - prompting him to ask: "Am I hearing that you think the staff should have better prepped you?"When she appeared on Fox & Friends, which Trump often watches, on Friday, Zacharia faced a similar line of questioning.She told the show's hosts that she did not disclose to Trump that she was not an attorney because "those questions weren't asked", saying she was hired for a communications role, not a legal one. Host Lawrence Jones then asked her: "Do you think you still have the confidence of the president?" She avoided offering a direct answer but ended by saying: "I hope to be able to build the confidence and trust of everyone around me."Zacharia's early exit is the quickest among Trump's White House press team.Anthony Scaramucci left his post as White House communications director after only 10 days during Trump's first term."Records are made to be broken," Scaramucci wrote on X on Friday. "But I take no pleasure in other people's pain."Prior to her appointment as press secretary, Zacharia was a frequent fixture on right-wing US networks such as Fox and Newsmax.She had a brief stint as a spokeswoman at the Department of Homeland Security (DHS) and worked as a communications adviser for Trump's social media platform Truth Social, according to her LinkedIn.In her early career, Zacharia worked as an intern for the Republican National Committee and the White House Office of Political Affairs during the Bush administration in 2006.

schema.headline: Katie Zacharia quits as White House press secretary five days into job

title: Three men jailed for 158 years each for murdering Australian brothers and US friend in Mexico
description: A Mexican judge has sentenced three men convicted of murdering Australian brothers Jake and Callum Robinson and their US friend Carter Rhoad to 158 ye
body: A Mexican judge has sentenced three men convicted of murdering Australian brothers Jake and Callum Robinson and their US friend Carter Rhoad to 158 years and nine months in jail each.The Robinsons and Rhoad were killed in an apparent botched robbery of their truck on a secluded beach in Baja California in 2024 while they were on a surfing trip, the court heard during the trial.The murders sent shockwaves around the world, particularly in Australia, as the area is usually safe from the violence seen in other parts of Mexico.The guilty verdict was handed down last week. Debra Robinson, the brothers' mother, told the courtroom that her sons' murders had taken "the future we had imagined with them".The convicted killers' full names were not given for legal reasons, meaning they were only identified as Jesús Gerardo, Irineo Francisco and Ángel Jesús.In November last year, the girlfriend of the alleged ringleader, Jesús Gerardo (alias "El Kekas"), was sentenced in a separate trial to 20 years in prison. She had admitted to involvement in the robbery.The court heard that the bodies of the victims were found dumped down a well with gunshot wounds to their heads.At the time, the murders shocked locals and tourists in the beach town of Ensenada who were disturbed at the apparent ease and sheer pointlessness of the killings.Ensenada has a reputation as a welcoming spot for surfers, but the chilling murders revealed how commonplace such extreme violence remains in Mexico.The only explanation the authorities were able to give was that the surfers - all in their early 30s - had ultimately been murdered for being in the wrong place at the wrong time.Their killings happened barely 36 hours after they crossed into Mexico from the US. Their bodies, however, were not found for another week, when their families were able to identify them.Local surfers also called for greater security for residents and visiting tourists, citing other recent examples of violence in the state. Tourism is a key part of the regional economy in Baja California.

schema.headline: Three men jailed for 158 years each for murdering Australian brothers and US friend in Mexico

title: Trial of German steakhouse heiress Christina Block that sparked a huge spy scandal
description: It is a trial that has gripped Germany, with a wealthy heiress in the dock for months and a case that triggered the country's biggest espionage scanda
body: It is a trial that has gripped Germany, with a wealthy heiress in the dock for months and a case that triggered the country's biggest espionage scandal in recent history.Christina Block, heir to a popular chain of steakhouses, is accused of ordering an Israeli security firm to carry out the violent abduction of her children from Denmark, following a bitter custody battle with her former husband.There are allegedly connections with at least two former secret agents, from Germany and Israel.In the latest twist, investigators in the case stumbled across evidence that has led to Germany's former intelligence chief, August Hanning, being arrested this month for treason and espionage.Hanning's arrest stunned the intelligence community. Although his case has nothing to do with the Hamburg trial, he has denied allegations of involvement in an earlier attempted abduction of the children.There was enormous media interest in Germany when Christina Block and six others went on trial in a high-security courtroom in Hamburg in July last year.Block House restaurants, specialising in steak and baked potatoes, are a feature of many German towns. Their success over the past half century has helped make Christina Block's father Eugen a multimillionaire.Prosecutors allege that she and a family lawyer, Andreas Costard, organised the forcible abduction of two of her children, who were staying with her former husband, Stephan Hensel, at his home in Denmark.They say the operation was carried out by a 36-year-old Israeli citizen named only as Jonathan G and five others.The abduction took place during the New Year celebrations of 2023-24, as the two children and their father were watching a firework display, according to the indictment.Prosecutors say several men ambushed and beat up Stephan Hensel, and dragged the boy and the girl, then 10 and 13 years old, into a car.On the approach to the border with Germany, they are alleged to have changed vehicles, taped up the children's mouths and tied the girl's hands.The group are then said to have travelled on to Baden-Württemberg in a campervan. Prosecutors say the children were held there against their will until their mother arrived to pick them up on 2 January 2024 and took them to her home in Hamburg.Christina Block, Andreas Costard and Jonathan G are charged with the abduction of minors, grievous bodily harm and unlawful detention.Block's partner, a former TV sports presenter called Gerhard Delling, and three others are charged with aiding and abetting.All of them deny wrongdoing, except for Jonathan G, who has admitted his involvement. However, he told the court he thought he was taking part in a rescue operation.The trial comes after years of legal battles between Christina Block and her former husband, Stephan Hensel, over who had the right to look after the children.Immediately after their separation, all four children lived with their mother in Hamburg. Hensel, who remarried, later moved to Denmark, where they regularly visited him.In 2021, the two youngest children went to visit their father in Denmark, but then were not brought back to Hamburg as agreed.A court in Hamburg ruled that Christina had custody and that the children should be returned. However, in February 2023, a Danish court ruled that, although the boy and the girl had been brought to Denmark unlawfully, they could not be taken back.In May 2023, Hensel was charged with the abduction of minors, in a case which is still pending.He has accused Christina of being violent with the children, charges she denies. She told the court Hensel wanted to take revenge on her.She also denied knowing anything about plans for the abduction of the children from Denmark. Her defence argues that the Israeli security team had acted on its own initiative.She told the court it was "a catastrophe" and that she had never wanted anything like that.The head of the Israeli security team, David Barkay, who is not on trial but faces future legal proceedings, told the court that Christina Block and Costard had known about the planned repatriation operation.Barkay, who was described by another witness as a former agent with Mossad, the Israeli secret service, said he had not shared all the details because he "didn't trust them."The alleged connection with Germany's former spy chief, August Hanning, relates to accusations of an earlier attempt to abduct the children and bring them back from Denmark in 2022.Prosecutors have said Hanning was responsible for arranging security staff sent to Denmark with Christina Block. His lawyer denies the accusations. Hanning has not been charged over the current Block court case.However, while investigators were searching his home, they came across evidence to suggest Hanning was involved in buying some 2,000 documents from his former chief of staff and then passing on state secrets to foreign powers. Which foreign power and who he is alleged to have given the secrets to is unspecified, but it has prompted widespread speculation.Now 80, Hanning is in custody charged with treasonous espionage. His lawyer says he is being "unjustly persecuted" and that the charges are "unfounded".Meanwhile the trial against Christina Block is currently on hold for two weeks - one of numerous delays and extensions over the course of the past 15 months.The latest delay is because a witness, Stephan Hensel's new wife, failed to appear in court.

schema.headline: Trial of German steakhouse heiress Christina Block that sparked a huge spy scandal

title: The uncertain future of Marineland's 30 rescued belugas
description: Tofino approached each of his handlers in turn as they knelt in shallow water and stroked his sides.Shortly after, a crane hoisted the more than 1,500
body: Tofino approached each of his handlers in turn as they knelt in shallow water and stroked his sides.Shortly after, a crane hoisted the more than 1,500kg beluga whale into a lorry to be shipped out of Canada to his new home, SeaWorld San Antonio - the last of 30 belugas and four dolphins to leave Marineland, a shuttered sea park near Niagara Falls.Marineland needed to find a new home for its whales. But when the Canadian government rejected its plan to sell them to China over concerns about animal welfare, the park's operations said they would have to be euthanised.That spurred an international rescue operation by several aquariums, leading to the largest ever transfer of captive whales this summer. But hopes that the animals were headed to a better life have been dampened by a number of deaths in the group.Photographer Carlos Osorio documented the move, which involved whales being flown to Chicago, Atlanta, San Diego, San Antonio and even Valencia in Spain.Osorio recalls watching footage from a drone overhead as Tofino appeared to say his own goodbyes.Tofino was the last captive whale in Canada. The country banned cetacean captivity and breeding seven years ago and Osorio felt the weight of the moment."This is the last one to happen and it's never going to happen again," he says.Despite the rescue operation, tragically, five of the belugas have since died, as well as one dolphin.Chicago's Shedd Aquarium has had the most deaths. Peekachu, 23, Rain, 20, Orisis, 26, and Caspian, 27, were all transferred from Marineland, while longtime Shedd resident Beethoven, 34, also died after eight Marineland belugas were brought there over the summer.Necropsies found chronic inflammatory disease in the gastrointestinal systems in Peekachu and Rain.Foreign objects were also discovered in their stomachs, including feathers, large rocks and flecks that appeared to be paint – objects Shedd believes were ingested before they were moved to Chicago.Osiris's preliminary examination identified chronic liver disease.Europe's largest aquarium, Oceanogràfic València in Spain, recorded the death of one beluga, Jelly Bean, and one dolphin, Echo. The dolphin arrived with "serious vision problems" and other health issues, it said, and "began having difficulties swallowing and respiratory problems" in the hours before she died.Experts say it is too early to judge the outcome of the transfers, especially considering the whales were facing euthanasia and had been living in an ageing facility. About 20 whales died at Marineland between 2019 and September 2025, according to a tally by the Canadian Press.Once the country's most popular amusement park, Marineland closed in 2024 after years of animal welfare concerns and financial woes following the death of its longtime owner.Public attitudes towards keeping whales in captivity have also changed drastically since Marineland opened in 1961. Like Canada, more countries are moving to ban or restrict the practice, including France and Mexico.Melissa Matlow, a spokeswoman for World Animal Protection Canada, says that worldwide there are about 3,600 captive cetaceans – a group of marine mammals that includes whales, dolphins and porpoises.But there are few alternatives for whales raised in captivity without the skills to survive in the wild.Matlow says that leaves a "growing animal welfare crisis on our hands".Still, her organisation had concerns about the relocation of the Marineland whales."If an animal was not healthy enough to withstand the stress of transport, it should not have been transported," she said in a statement. In early October, Shedd said it knew some of the Marineland belugas "could have substantial, longstanding medical needs".Assessments before the move "informed our planning but could not reveal every underlying condition or predict how each whale would respond to the transition. The rescue offered a path to continued, specialised care".They said the remaining belugas show positive signs, including eating well. World Animal Protection Canada had suggested two alternatives: repurpose Marineland into a hospice-style facility for the remaining captive whales and dolphins, or fast-track development of a proposed seaside sanctuary in Nova Scotia, the Whale Sanctuary Project.As they cannot be released, "the next best thing we could do is provide sanctuary for them, where they can at least live in the ocean, and they can have back their autonomy", says Lori Marino, a neuroscientist behind the Whale Sanctuary Project, which she hopes could eventually house about 12 to 15 whales."I look at it as an exit ramp," she adds.The project was initiated a decade ago, she said, but construction only began in the last two months. Fundraising is continuing and needs an additional C$6m ($4.2m; £3.1m).But offshore sanctuaries have yet to be proven a successful solution for retiring performing whales.One offshore facility for belugas is being created in Iceland, but in July organisers determined that more work was needed and delayed the introduction of two whales until next summer."They are kind of more theoretical and aspirational at this point," says Michael Weiss, research director at the Center for Whale Research in Washington state. He adds that they would definitely "improve the welfare of the animals" compared to concrete tanks."It's a very old idea," he says, noting that net pens have been used to rehabilitate injured wild whales, or temporarily used while re-introducing captured orcas back into the wild.Many critics note that Canada's law banning captivity also banned the breeding of whales - but the places where they were sent do not have the same laws and some are likely to breed them, perpetuating whale captivity.Jason Jones, senior curator of animal wellbeing at Georgia Aquarium, says "breeding is a natural part of an animal's life"."Breeding is part of good animal welfare, and so we want to make sure that they get the opportunity to do so."Georgia Aquarium recently took in two male Marineland belugas, named Balor, 10, and Zephyr, seven. They joined the four females already in their care.They arrived "bright, alert and responsive" and quickly began "vocalising to the females on the other side of the gate", he says."There was a little bit of a meeting and greeting period, but afterwards they were all kind of swimming together in a big group." "They were exploring their new habitat, coming over and participating in sessions, eating and interacting with enrichment. So those were all really positive signs from the get-go, and we've just seen progress since then."

schema.headline: The uncertain future of Marineland's 30 rescued belugas

title: Trump waives several Russia sanctions as row with Zelensky intensifies
description: Image source, ReutersByMax MatzaUpdated 6 hours agoDonald Trump has blocked numerous sanctions on Russia two days before they were due to take effect,
body: Image source, ReutersByMax MatzaUpdated 6 hours agoDonald Trump has blocked numerous sanctions on Russia two days before they were due to take effect, as a row with his Ukrainian counterpart Volodymyr Zelensky deepens.The sanctions were passed by the US Congress and signed into law by Trump in September.But the US president issued an executive order on Friday night saying that suspending some was in the US "national interest", prompting a backlash from US lawmakers. Zelensky said it was unfortunate the US has decided to "completely disregard" the sanctions.Relations between Washington and Kyiv frayed after the US struck a controversial deal to import Russian diesel last week. Ukraine then accused the Trump administration of withdrawing key military support.Trump and Zelensky have exchanged sharp words about one another. Ukraine's president declared it was nice to be among "real leaders" while addressing an EU summit, after Trump said Zelensky was "more difficult to deal with" than Russian President Vladimir Putin.The new US sanctions law took aim at Russia's economy, giving Trump broad powers to levy tariffs of up to 100% on imports from the top five purchasers of Russian oil and gas – most significantly China and India.It also included sanctions against senior Russian figures, including Putin, as well as Russian financial institutions and Moscow's so-called "shadow fleet" of vessels used to circumvent existing embargoes.Many of these provisions have now been waived by Trump.Russian envoy Kirill Dmitriev called the waiver "an important and truly historic moment".Posting on X, he said the sanctions would have inflicted "serious damage" primarily on the US and global market, and that economic cooperation benefits both nations.Democrats including the Virginia Congressman Don Beyer have criticised the move, accusing Trump of capitulating to Moscow and turning his back on Kyiv and Zelensky. "Trump's latest surrender to Putin again betrays our Ukrainian partners and defies clear congressional intent of legislation designed to punish Russia for its illegal war of aggression," Beyer wrote on X. The move is likely to draw further anger from Ukraine, where Zelensky has long stressed the need for stringent sanctions to limit funding Russia can use in its war effort.Zelensky said on Saturday morning that the sanctions "could have helped enormously" and that the law was "supposed to impose truly effective pressure on Russia to bring this war to an end".He pointed to Russian overnight attacks on 15 Ukrainian energy facilities that had caused power cuts in several regions and said: "Russia is trying to cause a blackout in Ukraine – right before winter."Zelensky said it was "important that everyone in America also sees what is really happening" on the ground.Figure caption, Watch: Will Ukraine get the support needed as tensions with US rise?He later told reporters that he believed the Trump administration would lift more sanctions against Russia.He also said negotiators Ukrainian spoke to their US counterparts on Friday and that both teams could meet next week.Trump was initially criticised by Zelensky and Ukraine's European allies for temporarily suspending some US sanctions to import Russian diesel in a bid to bring down US energy prices, which have skyrocketed during the Iran war.Trump has spent months grappling with the political consequences of the Middle East conflict, which has sent fuel costs soaring ahead of the US midterm elections. Rising inflation has soured Trump's standing with the American public.Zelensky suggested the deal was tantamount to the US investing in Russia's war effort.A few days later, Trump claimed that both Russia and Ukraine had agreed to an "energy ceasefire" to facilitate the export of Russian diesel. Both nations have been intensively striking one another's energy infrastructure. Kyiv says this is to limit revenue for Russia's war machine, while Moscow claims it only targets facilities used by the Ukrainian military.Zelensky initially expressed surprise at Trump's announcement, and said Kyiv would stop the strikes if Russia did the same. After three days which saw several fresh attacks from Russia, Kyiv resumed its strikes on Russian oil refineries.This prompted scathing condemnation from Trump, who called the strikes a "disgrace". Zelensky replied that he was "only standing up for Ukraine's interests". Image source, ReutersImage caption, Zaporizhzhia was among regions hit by Russian strikes overnightConcerns that Trump is siding with Russia have been heightened by disruption to a US-provided satellite system used by Ukraine.  Last week Starlink suddenly and unexpectedly restricted the speed at which drones could fly while still maintaining internet connection. This disrupted some battlefield missions, Ukraine said, and hampered Kyiv's ability to protect itself from incoming Russian attacks. During the slowdown, Russia launched several deadly strikes on Ukraine, with residents and the government saying these came with no prior warning.Zelensky told reporters on Saturday that Ukraine had been told by US officials the speed restrictions were linked to technical issues.However, he said Ukraine had tested Starlink on EU territory and found "these problems do not exist" and the system was operating at higher speeds.Trump has denied halting intelligence-sharing and deliberately slowing down Ukraine's Starlink network.Ukrainian authorities have confirmed that at least nine people have been killed and around 60 injured in Russian strikes across the country over the past 24 hours.They said an ambulance driver was killed and 20 others were injured in Russian strikes on the city of Kherson on Saturday morning.Russia's defence ministry said it had targeted industries linked to Ukraine's defence industry - including steel works, an electrical sub-station and a cargo vessel in the Black Sea.Additional reporting by Helen Sullivan

schema.headline: Trump waives several Russia sanctions as row with Zelensky intensifies

title: Jantar Mantar: Is this the end for iconic Delhi protest site?
description: A thousand slogans echoed here - but it could be the end for iconic Delhi protest siteImage source, ReutersImage caption, The "cockroach" demonstratio
body: A thousand slogans echoed here - but it could be the end for iconic Delhi protest siteImage source, ReutersImage caption, The "cockroach" demonstrations over the summer of 2026 could well become the last time Jantar Mantar was home to a sustained protest movement   BySharanya HrishikeshBBC News, DelhiWhat is the point of a protest?To raise your voice against injustice? To draw attention to a cause? Or to make those in power uncomfortable enough to listen?For more than three decades, Indians have tried to do all three in a narrow, tree-lined road near Jantar Mantar, an 18th Century astronomical obervatory in Delhi.But that may now be coming to an end.This week, Delhi Police said Jantar Mantar, located close to parliament, would no longer be a designated protest site.The decision comes months after the Gen Z-led Cockroach Janta Party (CJP) - not a political party but a collective which began as a joke - led a massive protest there demanding the resignation of federal education minister Dharmendra Pradhan. Tens of thousands turned up and Pradhan subsequently resigned.Police barricaded Jantar Mantar soon afterwards, preventing further demonstrations. Last week, an attempt by CJP supporters to march there, this time demanding the resignation of India's election chief, ended in a police crackdown.Protesters have now been directed to three other sites. Two are far from parliament, while the third, the sprawling Ramlila Ground, is often booked months in advance. Unlike Jantar Mantar, which is free, all three charge tens of thousands of rupees a day.Delhi Police says, external it acted after the Supreme Court suggested identifying alternative sites with adequate infrastructure. But critics say the move could push protests beyond the reach of ordinary Indians, further from the seat of power and into venues many cannot afford.Over the years, Jantar Mantar has witnessed everything from mass movements that shook governments to small, lonely demonstrations by people desperate to be heard. Farmers, students, grieving parents and ex-soldiers have gathered under its trees, holding placards and shouting slogans. Not every protest made headlines, but for many, it was a place to turn to when other doors had closed.This week, when the BBC visited, those scenes seemed a distant memory.Image source, Getty ImagesImage caption, Jantar Mantar is an 18th Century astronomical observatory in Delhi - the protests were held not in it, but in the road next to itYellow barricades blocked both ends of the road, with hundreds of paramilitary personnel standing guard, batons in hand.In a nearby lane, uniformed men sat in shops drinking tea or scrolling through their phones. At one of the few shops without policemen, the shopkeeper folded his hands and said he did not want to answer any questions.Built by Maharaja Sawai Jai Singh II in the 1720s, Jantar Mantar was once better known as a tourist attraction than a place where a thousand revolutions were imagined.Its story as a protest site began in 1993, when the then-Congress government stopped allowing demonstrations at the Boat Club lawns opposite the old parliament.Historian Harleen Kaur has traced how, from the 1960s onwards, successive governments brought in new rules that shifted the site of protest in Delhi further away from parliament."Jantar Mantar, situated 3km (1.86 miles) from the Parliament House, [allowed the government] to contain protesting crowds at some distance from the Parliament House and PM's residence," she wrote in a 2023 paper, external.Yet, the road saw countless spirited protests over the years.Rachna Dhingra, an activist with the Bhopal Group for Information and Action, an advocacy group for survivors of a 1984 gas leak disaster, camped at Jantar Mantar with hundreds of others for around five months in 2008, trying to get the government to agree to demands including setting up a commission to allocate resources for rehabilitation schemes.Through a scorching summer, they held press conferences, met politicians and even chained themselves to railings opposite then Prime Minister Manmohan Singh's residence to draw attention to their cause.It was also where she formed solidarities with others - Tibetans protesting against China, activists opposing the displacement of people over large dam projects and even just lone protesters who caught a train from their home towns with nothing but a placard and a grievance."It can be lonely to protest but that place became a home for so many of us. We shared each other's stories, struggles and victories," says Dhingra.Image source, Courtesy Rachna DhingraImage caption, In 2008, Rachna Dhingra and other activists camped for months at Jantar Mantar demanding justice for survivors of the deadly 1984 gas leak in Bhopal - when it rained, they sheltered under tarpaulin sheetsDipa Sinha, an academic associated with the Right to Food campaign, has seen ground-breaking laws - a landmark rural jobs guarantee scheme, the National Food Safety Act and Forest Rights Act - take shape at Jantar Mantar."It was a place where you could discuss issues with people who came to Delhi from across the country," she says.Protesters would demonstrate outside government offices, including the erstwhile Planning Commission and the agriculture ministry, where they were often detained by police, before returning to Jantar Mantar to "gather, discuss and strategise".But sustaining a protest for months was not easy.Dhingra says they sheltered under tarpaulin sheets when it rained, used public toilets near the site and went to nearby gurdwaras to freshen up.In 2017, the National Green Tribunal cited the lack of infrastructure, along with complaints from locals, to have Jantar Mantar shut down for protests.A year later, the Supreme Court overturned this, citing the rights to free speech and peaceful assembly guaranteed under the constitution.When asked whether the proximity to parliament made a difference to their cause, Dhingra quoted the reactions of her co-protesters who had come to Delhi for the first time."That's the president's house? Does the prime minister live there? How can they not listen to us when we are at their gates?" she remembered them saying.Sinha points out that Jantar Mantar was also near institutions like the Press Club and Constitution Club, making it easier to get media coverage, and for politicians to drop by and meet protesters.It was a simpler time - sometimes they would ask for permission from police only on the morning of the protest.Those rules have become much stricter, external now.In recent years, when Dhingra tried to protest at Jantar Mantar, she was told no-one could stay the night."Where do you go with hundreds of people who have travelled all the way to the capital to protest?" she asks.Image source, Getty ImagesImage caption, In 2006, Narmada Bachao Andolan (Save the Narmada river movement) leader Medha Patkar (grey sari), sat on a 20-day hunger strike at Jantar MantarImage source, Getty ImagesImage caption, In 2015, retired soldiers held protests at Jantar Mantar against the delay in the implementation of a pension schemeWhile Jantar Mantar has its supporters, others share memories of an even more vibrant protest culture.Mary E John, a gender studies scholar who lived in Delhi both as a student and as an academic, says that before 1993, she attended protests at the Boat Club on issues ranging from workers' rights and women's issues to topics of international significance."We lived in a climate where protest was part of life. In fact, we took it for granted," she says.When the spacious Boat Club lawns made way for Jantar Mantar, it actually felt "claustrophobic", she said.She pointed out that they, and others before and after them, protested at multiple sites - universities, colleges, streets - instead of just at Jantar Mantar.She sees signs of that in protests by farmers who camped at Delhi's borders for months, and people who sat at the Shaheen Bagh neighbourhood demanding the repeal of a controversial citizenship law.Even the 2012 anti-rape protests, she points out, were not restricted to Jantar Mantar but almost reached the Indian president's heavily guarded complex and beyond into other parts of Delhi.It's not clear what Jantar Mantar's future is - the Supreme Court is hearing pleas challenging its removal as a protest site.Opposition leader Rahul Gandhi and CJP leaders have said that Jantar Mantar belongs to the people and will be "reclaimed".As the debate rages on, Jantar Mantar is the quietest it has been in decades - will it hear slogans again?

schema.headline: Jantar Mantar: Is this the end for iconic Delhi protest site?

title: Three things we learned from the US midterm debates
description: What we learned from heated US midterm Senate debatesImage source, Getty ImagesImage caption, Susan Collins shakes Troy Jackson's handByAna FaguyWashi
body: What we learned from heated US midterm Senate debatesImage source, Getty ImagesImage caption, Susan Collins shakes Troy Jackson's handByAna FaguyWashington DCCandidates running for the US Senate in next month's midterm elections have taken to the debate stage over the past few weeks - with some heated exchanges and stinging personal attacks.As the 3 November election approaches and parties fight for control of Congress, some clear themes have emerged, particularly within some of the hotly-contested Senate races. Here's what you need to know.1. Not all Republicans are standing behind TrumpRepublicans running for office are facing the same question they have been asked in elections since 2016: how aligned are they with President Donald Trump?Conservatives who have bucked the president in the past have generally not fared well with voters. The president has seen low approval ratings in recent months, with polls suggesting voters are largely concerned with the cost of living and high fuel prices.While some Republican candidates have remained in lockstep with Trump, a Reuters analysis indicated, external that two-thirds of candidates in competitive US House and Senate races have broken with the president in some way this election cycle.Susan Collins, a Maine Republican running for her sixth term in the Senate who has repeatedly broken with Trump, is again putting clear distance between herself and the president. "I voted with President Biden 91% of the time," Collins said during a debate last week."The fact is, this year alone, this Congress alone, I voted against President Trump 137 times," she said.Collins is fighting a tighter Senate race than she expected against Democrat Troy Jackson, the former president of the Maine Senate. A New York Times/Siena University poll from mid-September suggests Collins could be ahead in that race by 3%, while others indicate Jackson is in the lead.Image source, Getty ImagesImage caption, Josh Turek (L) and Ashley HinsonElsewhere, some Republican candidates are choosing to separate themselves from the Trump administration's specific policy decisions, while expressing loyalty to Trump himself.In Iowa, traditionally a Republican stronghold, Congresswoman Ashley Hinson is facing a tougher-than-expected challenge in her Senate race.She is taking on Democrat Josh Turek, and some polls suggest he has a narrow lead.Hinson has not gone as far as Maine's Collins in separating herself from Trump, but she has broken with the president on some policy points.During a 13 October debate with Turek, Hinson was asked about the Trump administration striking a deal with Russia to import 300,000 tonnes to the US, followed by several other shipments.The Republican candidate did not mince her words: "We need to lower gas prices in this country, we need to lower diesel prices, but I don't think we need to be making a deal with Russia to do it."2. Personal attacks are a common themeAs they have debated in recent weeks, the candidates haven't held back on deploying pointed personal attacks against their opponents.The race for the vacant Michigan Senate seat - between rivals Abdul El-Sayed, a Democrat, and Mike Rogers, a Republican - has seen its fair share.Rogers, a Trump-backed former congressman, questioned during a debate whether anyone in his Muslim opponent's family might be on a "watchlist".El-Sayed, who would be the first Muslim member of the US Senate, pushed back strongly.He called the Republican "a sock puppet for the Trump administration" and said he was "weak, cowardly [and] won't stand up until his poll numbers drop".Image source, ReutersImage caption, Abdul El-Sayed (L) and Mike RogersOn Thursday, a protester interrupted the Maine debate and Collins suggested the disrupter was associated with her opponent. Jackson hit back at Collins: "Oh shut up, I don't even know that kid."Further south in Georgia, more personal attacks were exchanged between incumbent Democratic Senator Jon Ossoff and congressman Mike Collins, a Trump-backed Republican.What started as an exchange where Ossoff accused Collins of taking money out of Georgians' hands to give to data centre developers, quickly turned into a hurling of insults that included Ossoff calling Collins a "bigot" who has "hired half the Third Reich".Image source, ReutersImage caption, Mike Collins (L) and Jon OssoffIncendiary posts on social media from Collins' son-in-law, David Alan Scheer II, have become a point of contention in the race.In one post, Scheer blamed "Israel and Zionist Jews" for policies he said were intended to "undermine the white, Christian nature of America".Collins defended himself by accusing Ossoff of "spewing" "craziness"."I've condemned racism, antisemitism, hate; I don't care where the source is," the Republican said.3. Some candidates are skipping debates entirelyThere are 35 Senate seats up for grabs this November, but in 21 there are no debates scheduled among the main candidates, an ABC News analysis found.One race's lack of debates has surprised many observers: the Texas contest between James Talarico, a Democratic state representative, and Ken Paxton, a Republican and former state attorney general.Polls in the typically Republican state suggest that Talarico could be in reach of a surprise win. Should he succeed, he could help give Democrats control of the US Senate by flipping one of the four seats they need to create a majority.Talarico has accepted four debate invitations from different news networks. Paxton has not accepted any of those invitations. In July, Paxton's campaign spokesperson told media outlets he would debate Talarico. But since then, the campaign and Paxton have said little on the matter. Trump, who backed Paxton in the Republican primaries, has urged the candidates to debate."One thing about not showing up is you lose the opportunity to make the case for yourself, and instead, what you do is you give your opponent the ability and the opportunity to make your case as negative as possible," Peter Trumbore, a political science professor at Oakland University, told the BBC's US partner CBS News last month.Follow the twists and turns of Trump's second term with North America correspondent Anthony Zurcher's weekly US Politics Unspun newsletter. Readers in the UK can sign up here. Those outside the UK can sign up here.

schema.headline: Three things we learned from the US midterm debates

title: Pope discharged from hospital days after lung cancer surgery
description: Pope Leo XIV has been discharged from Rome's Gemelli Hospital, just four days after an operation to remove a cancerous growth from his lung.The 71-yea
body: Pope Leo XIV has been discharged from Rome's Gemelli Hospital, just four days after an operation to remove a cancerous growth from his lung.The 71-year-old walked unaided to his waiting car, stopping to speak to well-wishers.The Vatican said the Pope will give the traditional Angelus prayer and blessing to a crowd in St Peter's Square on Sunday, as he did last week when he surprised the world by announcing the surgery.On Friday, photographs were released of the Pope celebrating Mass and distributing communion in hospital for staff. A statement from his doctors said blood tests and a chest X-ray showed "steady improvement" following his operation.The surgery on Tuesday, which lasted for 90 minutes, included the removal of the lower lobe of the Pope's right lung. The results of further tests to check for any sign that the cancer has spread have not yet been announced.The Pope also spoke to Russian President Vladimir Putin on Friday, in their first call since June 2025. The Vatican said the call was to urge "dialogue and peace".It came as Russia's bombardment of cities across Ukraine intensifies, with a growing number of civilian casualties and no sign of Putin being ready to halt the invasion.The Pope also called for a humanitarian ceasefire in the Ukrainian city of Oleshkiy, occupied by Russia and under constant shelling, to allow people to be evacuated and for the urgent delivery of food and medicine. The BBC recently reported on residents there being forced to eat garden weeds to survive.The Pope's schedule has been cleared completely until 20 October, so his reappearance in public so soon is a surprise and will be some relief for Catholics around the world.Those close to the Pope said he was keen not to delay a trip to Latin America, planned for early November and which includes a visit to Peru, where he was a missionary for many years.It is not yet clear whether he might be fit to travel or require further treatment.

schema.headline: Pope discharged from hospital days after lung cancer surgery

title: Judge throws out child sex abuse charges against actor Timothy Busfield
description: State District Judge Joseph Montano granted the defence's motion to dismiss the indictment on Friday, citing mistakes that undermined the grand jury p
body: State District Judge Joseph Montano granted the defence's motion to dismiss the indictment on Friday, citing mistakes that undermined the grand jury process."Our office has received the order and is evaluating our options to determine how we will proceed," a spokesperson for the Office of the Second Judicial District Attorney in Bernalillo County told the BBC on Friday.The BBC has contacted a legal representative for Busfield.The actor surrendered to state authorities in January when a warrant was issued for his arrest. A judge later ordered his release pending trial.Busfield had originally been taken into custody in Albuquerque on two counts of criminal sexual contact with a minor and one count of child abuse.The indictment against him, reviewed by the BBC, said that on or between 19 October 2022 and 10 September 2023, Busfield "touched or applied force to the intimate parts" of one of the unnamed boys when he was under the age of 13.The Thirtysomething actor's defence team submitted more than 70 letters from people vouching for his character and said that he underwent and passed a polygraph test pertaining to the allegations against him.In a warrant for Busfield's arrest, prosecutors had said the parents of the boys alleged that he groomed and sexually abused the youngsters while working on The Cleaning Lady.Authorities claimed the boys referred to Busfield as "Uncle Tim" and alleged that he "would tickle them on the stomach and legs". Both boys told authorities they were touched inappropriately for years, his arrest affidavit stated.Busfield's lawyers had said the actor was being accused as an act of revenge after the children were fired from the series, which angered their mother.Additional reporting by Nardine Saad

schema.headline: Judge throws out child sex abuse charges against actor Timothy Busfield

title: Brazil sees record fall in Amazon deforestation as key election looms
description: Jair Bolsonaro promoted mining in indigenous lands in the Amazon and forest clearances soared at the same time as resources to protect the forest were
body: Jair Bolsonaro promoted mining in indigenous lands in the Amazon and forest clearances soared at the same time as resources to protect the forest were cut.During Bolsonaro's presidency from 2019 to 2022, the Amazon lost nearly 60% more in forest lands compared to the previous four years, news agency AFP reported, citing official data.Lula reversed his policies and oversaw deforestation rates drop to a six-year low during his first year in office. Lula tightened up environmental monitoring and penalties for illegal logging."Our goal is to achieve zero illegal deforestation by 2030," he said in a post on X on Friday.Tropical rainforests like the Amazon are home to millions of species. In a healthy state, they absorb vast quantities of planet-warming carbon dioxide, helping to keep the Earth cool.But they have come under increasing pressure from decades of deliberate land clearance for agriculture and logging, as well as climate change, which scientists warn can create conditions for wildfires.Brazil's Environment Minister Joao Paulo Capobianco described the decline in Amazon deforestation as "absolutely stratospheric".It was an "historic achievement" for Brazil, said Marcio Astrini, executive secretary at climate advocacy group Observatorio do Clima.It showed that "with political will, it is possible to curb deforestation and greenhouse gas emissions", Astrini said.

schema.headline: Brazil sees record fall in Amazon deforestation as key election looms

title: Actress Selma Blair says she 'did not intend to harm anyone' in plane altercation
description: Blair's publicist described the actress's physical achievements since her MS diagnosis as "nothing short of a miracle" and said she still lives with p
body: Blair's publicist described the actress's physical achievements since her MS diagnosis as "nothing short of a miracle" and said she still lives with pain daily. "Selma had never been arrested before Sunday night," she said. "There is much more to this story than has been reported and we ask to consider the entirety of the facts before rushing to judgement, whether in the courtroom or in the court of public opinion."The incident happened on a flight travelling from Los Angeles to New York on Sunday evening. New York airport officials responded to a call about "a physically abusive passenger" on a Delta Airlines flight. Two flight attendants were hurt and one was taken to hospital, the New York Port Authority said.A pilot asked for medical help, describing "a bloody nose" and "some bite marks", according to audio recorded on air traffic control obtained by CBS News, the BBC's US partner.Blair was arrested and taken to hospital. She was issued a federal summons by the FBI for a charge of assault within the special maritime and territorial jurisdiction of the US that relates to the on-board altercation.The two additional charges of assault were filed in state court after she was taken off the plane. She has pleaded not guilty to those charges and was released on bail. Additional reporting by Rebecka Pieder

schema.headline: Actress Selma Blair says she 'did not intend to harm anyone' in plane altercation

title: Trump 'completely wrong' to restrict support for Ukraine, Italian minister tells BBC
description: Italy's defence minister has said it was a "complete mistake, a major mistake" for the US to limit access to satellite systems and intelligence used b
body: Italy's defence minister has said it was a "complete mistake, a major mistake" for the US to limit access to satellite systems and intelligence used by Ukraine to defend itself against Russian attacks.Guido Crosetto warned in a BBC interview that any such move by US President Donald Trump's administration "makes absolutely no sense" and risked prolonging Russia's full-scale invasion rather than helping to bring peace. Trump has denied asking for satellite access to be suspended.Crosetto's comments continue Italy's sharpening criticism of the US.Earlier this week, Prime Minister Giorgia Meloni called Trump's deal to buy diesel from Russia a "very risky choice" and said it would "grant Russia legitimacy" as it bombed cities in Ukraine.Trump agreed the deal with Russian President Vladimir Putin, blaming Kyiv's own attacks on Russian refineries for rising fuel prices.Meloni, once considered so close to the US president she was dubbed a "Trump whisperer", said the move ran counter to efforts to bring Putin to the negotiating table."Peace will come when Putin is convinced there is a stalemate, that he cannot advance any further," her defence minister told the BBC at his ministry building in Rome.Crosetto was a co-founder of Meloni's hard-right Fratelli d'Italia party, which has led a right-wing government coalition since 2022, shortly after the start of Russia's full-scale war."If [Putin] sees weakness on the Ukrainian side – and if the US deprives Ukraine of resources, that creates weakness – then he will believe he can win. So he will continue the war," Crosetto warned."I think that is completely wrong."Despite widespread public scepticism, Meloni's Italian government has been a strong ally of Ukraine from the start, sending both military and humanitarian aid.The specifics of those deliveries have always been classified.Crosetto said that victory for Ukraine would be "a victory for peace, a victory for justice, a victory for international law".He vowed that Italian military support would continue "for as long as this government is in place", though he warned that getting Italy's parliament to approve further deliveries would be "more difficult" as elections approached.The vote has to take place by the end of 2027 and opinion polls currently put a new far-right party, Futuro Nazionale, ahead of all Meloni's coalition partners.That party's leader, former general Roberto Vannacci, is openly sympathetic to Russia and opposes aiding Ukraine, arguing that Europe is wasting its money as Russia's military "continues to advance" on the ground.At a recent event in Tuscany, he described himself as "neither pro-Putin nor pro-Russian" but "pro-Italian".Crosetto brushed off questions about Vannacci, including on whether his views reflected those of many Italians, saying he had more "serious matters to deal with".But, perhaps to underline the difference, he was unequivocal on Russia."When one state crosses another state's border with tanks, when it bombs hospitals and schools, kills civilians and bombs power plants, and has been doing so for four years, I can only describe that as evil," he said.Italians, like many Europeans, are seeing prices go up, driven by the high cost of energy.During street protests in Rome on Friday, where firecrackers were thrown, secondary school students complained that resources were being diverted to arms instead of education.Some chanted: "We want more classroom, not more bombs."In southern Italy, truckers have begun blocking roads complaining at the hike in fuel prices.Polls here regularly show that a majority of Italians want an end to military aid for Ukraine. One, conducted for the Ixè institute in September, put support for continuing to supply arms at just 18%.There are many factors behind that, from a long-standing pacifist tradition to a history of strong business ties to Moscow. Unlike Poland or the Baltic states, Italy feels physically distant from the danger, too.But the defence minister also blamed an active campaign of disinformation by Moscow – targeting, he said, "certain political figures... and narratives to weaken the political climate against Russia"."In some way they shift public opinion," the minister argued."It's very hard to explain to a citizen who's having trouble at the petrol pump that we can't give any concessions to Russia right now. But that's the only way to defend the future of that very citizen who's complaining."Italy has not been targeted for major acts of sabotage, unlike other allies of Ukraine in Europe.The minister said a fire at an arms depot outside Rome in August was not arson, but "human stupidity".A report last month that Russia was planning to launch drone attacks at Italy, France and Spain from the container ships in the Mediterranean was not proven, Crosetto also told us.But cyber-attacks, which he linked to Russia, were now routine - "there are hundreds every day" - and he believed Europe had been too weak in its response."You can't win a war... if you don't fight back," the minister said.Additional reporting from Rome by Davide Ghiglione

schema.headline: Trump 'completely wrong' to restrict support for Ukraine, Italian minister tells BBC

title: Inside Ukrainian offensive pushing Russia back - with Starlink playing a key role
description: Figure caption, Watch: BBC follows Ukraine's Operation Vivaldi pushing Russia back on frontlineByDan JohnsonUkraine correspondentReporting fromnear Ly
body: Figure caption, Watch: BBC follows Ukraine's Operation Vivaldi pushing Russia back on frontlineByDan JohnsonUkraine correspondentReporting fromnear Lyman, eastern UkraineA Russian drone zips across the computer screen, startling the commanders keeping watch over the battlefield via a live stream in their bunker.Cigarette in one hand, radio in the other, one of them calls in their own drone to bring it down and warns the soldiers below of the threat. The men are dangerously exposed, on the long walk across open ground from their front line positions. They are being replaced after three months forcing the Russians back.This is part of Operation Vivaldi, a Ukrainian counter-offensive which they say has liberated 277 sq km (106 square miles) in the eastern Donbas region in recent months. The name reflects the offensive's four stages, or seasons - like the Italian composer's violin concerto. The successful assault blunted an attempted Russian pincer movement that threatened to encircle the key Fortress Belt cities still under Ukrainian control.While Russia this month pummels Ukraine from the air, crippling its energy infrastructure and killing scores of civilians across the country, at the front, it is Ukraine that has made recent gains. Kyiv says it has inflicted heavy losses - 8,000 Russian casualties in Vivaldi alone, and close to 50,000 along the front in the month of September –  and suffered few casualties in return.Image source, ReutersImage caption, The Starlink system was integrated into Ukraine's Operation Vivaldi, but this week Kyiv said restrictions had been imposed on it without warningThe Institute for the Study of War reported that pro-Russian military bloggers had acknowledged the Ukrainian advances, and expressed fears this could lead to more losses for Russia in the future. No Russian official has publicly acknowledged the Ukrainian gains. Russian ministry of defence briefings say only that they were "repelling attacks" in the Lyman region, or "improving the tactical position at the front".Despite Ukraine's forward moves, Russian drones are still ever-present. Phoenix, Commandant of the Revenge Brigade's Silver Trinity unit, tells me his men face 10 on an average day.Image caption, Ukraine's military says it has liberated 277 sq km in the eastern Donbas regionHe is fixed on the live stream as a Ukrainian snare swoops in, hovers for a few seconds and drops a net on to the drone, dragging it from the sky. This Russian drone was for reconnaissance, but if it had locked on to the soldiers, another drone carrying explosives would have followed.This moment of peril illustrates the layers making up the modern battlefield. The command bunker receives live pictures from a hovering camera, while below a Ukrainian attack drone attacks another enemy spotter which would have called in more flying firepower.Integrated in all of this is Starshield, the military version of Elon Musk's Starlink satellite communications network, providing broadband connectivity across the battlefield.Ukraine said this week, as Operation Vivaldi concluded, that the system had restrictions imposed without warning, limiting their capability. Musk and media reports suggest the order may have come from the White House. While Ukraine is not wholly reliant on Starshield, it is a key tool in their arsenal, vital for interceptor and mid-range strike drones. And knowing this tool can be restricted without any warning or consultation has sparked major concern in Ukraine.Beneath the battle for aerial superiority, unmanned ground vehicles scurry back and forth delivering supplies, evacuating the wounded or, increasingly, leading the charge against the enemy.Everything here relies on digital connectivity - to see, to move, to fly, to communicate, to fire. But at the bottom of this stack, it is still human beings in trenches who are holding the ground.The weary soldiers have made it safely to the command post. After 95 days pushing forward on the front line there is an emotional reunion.Image source, Matthew Goddard/BBCImage caption, Dealer, a soldier in the Revenge Brigade's Silver Trinity unit, just came off the front lineAn infantryman with the call-sign Dealer tells me he feels strong, but it is good to be finally heading home: "It's an impressive operation. Over three months, we moved positions four times."He tells me the most frightening threat was Russian drones, piloted remotely and determined to hunt down their target.Commandant Phoenix said the preparation for the offensive was "enormous"."The men trained for months. We had to completely restructure our approach because previously we had been defending, and now we had to go on the offensive."Robots and drones led the assault on Russian positions and, for the first time, remote-controlled explosive vehicles were dropped behind Russian lines - 250 Russians surrendered. According to Ukrainian commanders, their year-long campaign has freed 16 settlements from Russian occupation.Image source, Matthew Goddard/BBCImage caption, Phoenix, Commandant of the Revenge Brigade's Silver Trinity unitIn Karpivka, a village occupied since April, the Ukrainians found one local resident remaining - 61 year old Volodymyr Zamota, the last man standing when his neighbours fled the Russian advance in 2025. He says he survived for eight months in total isolation."As they say, hope dies last," he told me. "I'm the only person left in the whole village, and the village has been almost completely destroyed.""I thought I would live to old age without experiencing anything like this, but then it happened. It's a terrible tragedy".That devastation defines the region Ukraine has just recaptured. It's still too risky for residents to return, if they even have a home intact. But Ukraine's soldiers are celebrating this regained ground, the halted Russian advance and the future potential this operation may present."The real value of this is securing advantageous positions, favourable lines, and a bridgehead that grants us a superior position," Andriy Hitt, Revenge Bridge chief of staff, explained."This allows us to create the necessary conditions for subsequent successful operations, seize the initiative in battle, and plan future successful manoeuvres… each of these actions is a building block towards victory."Image source, Matthew Goddard/BBCImage caption, Nets now span roads in eastern Ukraine to protect from dronesAll this could be threatened by the limitations on US technology, and American intelligence. Relations between Kyiv and Washington are at an all-time low.This week President Zelensky said he felt "betrayed" by Donald Trump, while the US leader declared he was "not a fan" of his Ukrainian counterpart, saying he was harder to deal with than Vladimir Putin. Trump says Ukraine's strikes on Russian oil refineries have hiked oil prices. Ukraine says the US and Israeli war against Iran is the cause.But despite the diplomatic divisions, among the soldiers we met, morale is high. Dealer says Operation Vivaldi has renewed his belief Ukraine can win the war.The unit is ensuring Volodymyr, Grandpa as they call him, has enough to eat - drones drop off food parcels on their way to feed soldiers at the front.I asked Volodymyr if he believed Ukraine could win. "Yes, of course I do. I would just like to know when it will happen, when all of this will finally end."Additional reporting by Kostas Kallergis and Anastasiia Levchenko

schema.headline: Inside Ukrainian offensive pushing Russia back - with Starlink playing a key role

title: Social media algorithms: What if you could turn them off?
description: Toxic algorithms wouldn't let them go - now Australia wants an off switchFigure caption, Watch: Many social platforms already have following-only feed
body: Toxic algorithms wouldn't let them go - now Australia wants an off switchFigure caption, Watch: Many social platforms already have following-only feeds - here's how they workByTiffanie TurnbullSydneyWarning: This article contains an account of living with an eating disorderVarsha Yajman was already self-conscious about the way she looked when she joined social media as a 13-year-old.Endless workout videos making impossible promises filled her feeds. Through the screen, girls she'd never met urged her to sign up to dangerous calorie challenges. Others proudly promoted their height and weight - even the number of times they had been sent to hospital - on their profiles in a form of twisted competition.Every night as she fell asleep, Varsha would watch a stranger on the internet diarising what they'd consumed that day."I was like, 'I don't need to eat. I can just watch other people eat'," Varsha tells the BBC."I would find that I'd be down these really deep rabbit holes... it was like no matter how hard you tried to get out, you couldn't."Now 24 and in recovery from anorexia, Varsha says she is still served weight loss content on social media - despite having every safety setting turned on, and an exhaustive list of banned words.Image source, Tiffanie Turnbull / BBCImage caption, Varsha Yajman says social media aggravated her eating disorderIt is people like her the Australian government says it is trying to protect with a new suite of laws cracking down on big tech, which were introduced to parliament this week.The centrepiece of their proposed reforms: an algorithm switch which would force social media platforms to let users turn off recommender content. The idea is that you would only see posts from accounts you follow.It isn't the first government to try this, but existing algorithm controls are often transient and come with trade-offs in app functionality.Australia has set out to make its legislation tighter to stop this. And it hopes its new laws – which would also impose a legal duty of care on online services – will help Australians become happier and healthier.But critics are concerned Prime Minister Anthony Albanese's government has bitten off more than it can chew in its fight with big tech, while others, including the Trump administration, say the reforms threaten free speech.The choiceFlynn Martin knows what it is like to be sucked into an algorithmic spiral.Self-proclaimed misogynist influencer Andrew Tate and other manosphere figures started overwhelming the then-20-year-old's social media feeds about four years ago.It was a time when Flynn, who was eventually diagnosed with bipolar disorder, was insecure, frustrated with his life and struggling with his mental health. He says he fell for the rhetoric.He soon went viral in Australia for two videos: one ranting about whether it was OK to be a straight white male, and another where he criticised a date for her frozen yoghurt order."You find yourself in like a bit of an echo chamber... It's easy to get swept up in that," he tells the BBC."I really bought into the idea we were living in this matrix, we had this really negative system that was designed against you. And the only way to break out of it was becoming this alpha male character."The Melbournian was only pulled from the manosphere after a period of psychosis and a hospital stay.Image source, Daniel Fermer / ABC NewsImage caption, Flynn Martin says he's still finding a healthy balance with social mediaNowadays, he finds it tough to look back at that version of himself: "While there's a bit of shame and embarrassment... I think there is a bit of empathy for that younger man."Both Flynn and Varsha know social media alone isn't to blame for the worst chapter of their lives, but say it was a key factor.Countless others have stories of being confronted by social media content they didn't seek out, and didn't want to see – and there's long been suspicions the algorithms curating these platforms are harming users.Social media firms argue the potential risks are being overstated and that they already provide users with effective safety tools.But research emerging from around the world has been sketching a different picture.Studies have found social media use triggers a similar brain response to gambling and substance addiction, external; that algorithms – often unsolicited – serve up content which harms users' mental health, external, and that they're spreading disinformation and increasing polarisation, driving violence offline.Court cases and whistleblowers have aired claims that these companies know the dangers and are willing to overlook them as this technology lifts user engagement and their bottom line."The result is that they promote content that is outrageous or that invokes strong emotions from people - so it might be anger or fear or desire or lust or insecurity, whatever it is, it's going to keep us scrolling," Chanel Contos tells the BBC.Image source, Cordelia Hsu/ReutersImage caption, Consent education campaigner Chanel Contos lobbied the government for change after founding the Teach Us Consent website in 2021While studying the topic at university, the activist - who helped reform sexual consent education standards in Australia - came up with a campaign for change."Fix Our Feeds" demanded recommended algorithms be turned off by default, and social media users be given the choice to opt into them.Contos envisaged a nostalgic return to the social media of the early 2010s – a time when a person's social media was filled with posts from friends or people they actually followed and their feeds were finite.More than 15,000 people signed her petition, and the campaign also won the backing of two former prime ministers, several MPs, influential figures, mental health advocates, and online safety experts.The government in September said it had listened to the Australians who had backed Contos's campaign, and announced a version of her proposal: forcing big tech to introduce an algorithm switch - but stopping short of requiring it be automatically set to off."This is not about giving government control, it is about giving people control," Albanese said."If people want to doom scroll… that's fine, that's up to them."Image source, Hilary Wardhaugh/Getty ImagesImage caption, Communications Minister Anika Wells (left podium) and Australian PM Anthony Albanese (right podium) announcing the upcoming Digital Duty of Care bill The policy is part of the government's Digital Duty of Care bill, which would require online services – social media firms, gaming sites, chatbots and more – to "ensure, so far as is reasonably practicable, a safe online environment".Children must be protected from "harmful" material and design features – for example, pornography and material which encourages eating disorders or harmful attitudes towards women – and adults must be protected from "seriously harmful" material and conduct, a much narrower list of illegal content. Breaches of the law could attract fines of up A$100m (£52m, $70m)."The digital duty of care answers a lot of the 'what abouts' of the social media minimum age law because it's much broader; it captures all online services and it shifts the onus of responsibility from the shoulders of victims onto the shoulders of the big tech operators who seek to make money off Australian users," Communications Minister Anika Wells told the BBC.The challengesThere's been a muted response from big tech. Meta, Snap, TikTok, X and Google, which owns YouTube, have all declined BBC requests for comment, and have not made public statements about the legislation.In the days after the announcement, Instagram boss Adam Mosseri argued non-algorithmic feeds would mean users saw fewer posts from friends, and said he didn't believe his app was addictive – although a US jury recently ruled otherwise."I think we conflate the way we colloquially use the word 'addicted' – like, 'I'm addicted to this show, and I'm binge-watching it' – and clinical addiction," he told a press briefing in Sydney.Image source, Jason Henry/Bloomberg via Getty ImagesImage caption, Instagram chief Adam Mosseri argues recommender algorithms are essential to user enjoymentRight-wing parties in Australia – and the Trump administration – have said the algorithms proposal and the broader bill both risk forcing over-moderation and censorship.But those who defend the law say that won't happen because you can still follow who you want and share what you want. "If adults listen to manosphere podcasts, or people post their views about the government, or make memes, or want to say the moon landing was fake – they can continue to do so without restriction," Wells said this week.The proposal seems to be far less divisive amongst the public and online safety experts compared with Australia's social media ban for children.However, the big question is: how will Australia implement this policy when, so far, it has been struggling to implement the ban? Surveys suggest most children who were on social media before the ban still are, and no fines have been issued.Image source, Getty ImagesImage caption, Australian regulators are investigating potential breaches of the social media banThe EU's attempt at introducing algorithm controls in 2023 – after which platforms rolled out following-only feeds – is a cautionary tale.Social media firms have indicated the take-up of safety and control features like this has been low and cite it as evidence users like their products the way they are. Experts say there is a reason for that."Platforms do what the law orders, but in such a clunky way that users don't actually enjoy the option and stick with the default, algorithmic experience," researcher Chris Zomer, from the ARC Centre of Excellence for the Digital Child, wrote in The Conversation, external.On Instagram for example, when you turn off the algorithm, you can't see direct messages or access your profile and settings. When you leave the app, it reverts back to an algorithm-governed feed on your return.The only place where these issues don't exist is the Netherlands. It was changed there after a Dutch court last year found Meta in breach of the EU's Digital Services Act.Image source, Benjamin Fanjoy/Bloomberg via Getty ImagesImage caption, Meta lost an appeal against the Dutch court's ruling in March, meaning users in the Netherlands retain choice over their home feedsThe rules for Australia aren't set in stone yet, but the government says following-only feeds must not be harder to use or less functional, that algorithm settings must be "obvious", and that they must not change without an "explicit choice" by the user, even if they leave the app.Buoyed by her success in Australia, Contos is now taking her campaign global."We feel like Canada, UK, Australia are all very aligned on online safety... Then if those three jurisdictions are doing it, it could become a critical mass thing."Though experiences like theirs helped inspire these reforms, both Flynn and Varsha are somewhat sceptical of them.Varsha says she struggles to believe a country like Australia can outmuscle big tech: so she's not sure the Digital Duty of Care bill will work. And Flynn says lawmakers should be "realistic" about the potential of the algorithm switch: "At the end of the day we use social media as a form of entertainment."Polling earlier this month indicated two-thirds of their fellow Gen-Zs would keep their social media algorithms – though nearly half of Australians more generally would turn theirs off.Though Varsha admits she is unlikely to make much use of an algorithm switch, she appreciates having the choice."On a bad day I'm still susceptible to all of the things that I was at 17. To know that, if I'm having a bad day, I can opt out makes me feel really good."If you've been affected by the issues raised in this story, you could speak to a health professional or an organisation that offers support. Details of organisations offering advice and support for people in the UK are available from BBC Action Line.

title: Oregon teacher fought school attacker before armed dad killed suspect

body: Some readers may find this article distressing.A female teacher in the US state of Oregon tackled a teenage shooter who entered her classroom and tried to wrestle the gun from his grasp, police have said.The teacher, who has not been named, threw her mobile phone before trying to disarm the 16-year-old on the floor of a classroom at Silver Rail Elementary in the city of Bend.The attacker killed three children and a teacher after shooting his way into the building on Thursday.He was shot dead by a father with two daughters at the school, who was driving past as the attack started to unfold and, armed with a pistol, ran in to confront the suspect.Police said the attacker used to be a student at the school. His motive remains unclear.He had been armed with about 44 more rounds of shotgun ammunition when he was stopped, police said. He fired as many as 15 rounds in the class. "To the people who showed courage in the face of such violence and intervened to prevent this tragedy from being any worse, we owe you a debt of gratitude," Bend Police Chief Mike Krantz said.Police used a news conference on Friday to identify two of the four victims of the school shooting. They were five-year-old Rhoam Summer and 25-year-old teacher Meghan Lambert.Lambert's family said in a statement shared by the police that her goal was to be a teacher in the district in which she grew up and that she was "compassionate and had a huge heart"."She always fought for the underdog and those with special needs," they said.Bryan Jolly, Summer's grandfather, said the family was devastated by his death."The whole thing is senseless, and a shock," he told the New York Times, saying his grandson was "was very bright and very mischievous and very fun-loving, and totally without fear".The families of the two other students who were killed, an eight-year-old and 11-year-old, did not wish to have them publicly identified yet, police said. Two others were injured in the attack. Another teacher, a 54-year-old, was still being treated at hospital, and a seven-year-old student, who was in serious but stable condition. Krantz said the heroic actions of both the teacher and the father who ran inside the school had saved lives.He said the teacher who wrestled with the gunman had not been hurt but "almost certainly helped prevent more bloodshed". Krantz identified the suspect as 16-year-old Griffin J John II, who had been a special educational needs student at the school. A search warrant has been executed at his home and a search is ongoing, the police chief said.Police believe the suspect travelled to the elementary school on foot, but they are still investigating his exact movements and how he acquired the gun.Officials did not confirm the name of the father who intervened and fatally shot the suspect.But Kaylub Giamanco's family has identified him to US media as the person who sprang into action.The 36-year-old carpenter had just finished lunch and was on his way home when he passed the school, his brother told NBC News. He saw the suspect open fire on a vehicle outside the school and then shoot through a window to gain entry. Police said he had a legally concealed .40 calibre in his vehicle, while his brother said he grabbed the pistol "and decided to go in after" the suspect. Police say he fired at the suspect "multiple times", killing him. Giamanco's mother, Kenda Freeman, who lives in Sacramento, California, told a local CBS station that her son had called her moments after the shooting and that he was "traumatised"."He said 'a man went into my daughter's school'," Freeman recalled, pausing as she started to tear up. "And, um, shot kids. And he said, 'and I looked at him point blank, and I shot and killed him, mum'."She added: "I told him he saved a lot of lives, and he said, 'mum, I couldn't save them all'."US President Donald Trump praised the bystander on Friday, calling him a "great hero" and telling reporters that the situation could have become "much worse"."It's a terrible thing, but thank goodness for a man that had a gun and knew how to use it," he said.Without naming the bystander, Oregon Governor Tina Kotek acknowledged the man's heroic actions as having stopped further loss of life, but noted they "carry a heavy emotional burden and I just want you to know that my thoughts are with you as well".Additional reporting by Kayla Epstein
